opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that it almost never looks like the clean story you read in the paper. The paper is written backwards: you start from the conclusion and build a neat staircase to it. But the actual process is much messier. You wander, you try things that don't work, you get stuck for weeks, and sometimes the thing that eventually matters was sitting in a side experiment you almost threw away.

For me, a lot of good research comes from holding on to a question for a long time, often longer than is comfortable. I'll have some nagging feeling that the field's default assumption is a bit off, or that we're explaining a result with the wrong story. That feeling doesn't turn into a project right away. It sits in the background. Then you read something, or a student shows you an odd plot, or you have a conversation with someone in a completely different area, and suddenly a few pieces that seemed unrelated click together. From the outside it looks like a jump. From the inside it's more like slow accumulation followed by a sudden phase change.

So I've learned not to be too impatient with the nonlinear part. When you're in the middle of it, it feels like you're wasting time, because there's no visible progress. But a lot of that "wasted" time is where you build intuition: you learn what doesn't work and why, and that becomes the foundation for the moment when something finally does.

Another thing I care about a lot is being willing to question what everyone treats as settled. In fast-moving fields there's a strong pull to follow the trend, scale up the current recipe, and add a bit on top. That's useful work, but some of the most interesting results come from stepping back and asking, "Is this component actually necessary? What if we strip it down? What are we really measuring?" Often the answer is surprising, and that surprise is a signal that you've found something real.

And it's very much a collective process. Many of the turns in a project come from students and collaborators: someone ran an experiment I wouldn't have thought to run, or pushed back on an idea I was too attached to. Part of my job is creating an environment where people feel free to explore, make mistakes, and follow strange observations, instead of everyone just optimizing toward a predefined target.

So if I had to summarize: good research, for me, is a mix of long-term curiosity, tolerance for confusion, a bit of stubbornness about questioning assumptions, and luck. The nonlinearity isn't a bug in the process. It's kind of the process itself.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I don't think I've ever had a project where the path looked anything like the paper that came out of it. The paper is a story we tell afterward. It has a motivation, a method, experiments, a clean arc. The actual process is much messier than that.

Usually it starts with a feeling that something is off. Not a hypothesis, just discomfort. With ConvNeXt, for example, the starting point was not "let's modernize ConvNets." It was more like sitting with the fact that vision transformers were winning, and feeling that the explanation everyone gave, attention, didn't fully add up. We couldn't say why, we just didn't believe it. So you poke at it. You run a lot of experiments that go nowhere. You spend weeks on a direction, it fails, and then something you noticed as a side effect three weeks earlier suddenly becomes the real thing.

I think the key is that you can't plan your way to the insight. You can only put yourself in the position to recognize it when it shows up. That means a few things. You need to keep running experiments even when you don't have a clear story, because the data will tell you something you weren't asking about. You need to have deep, slow conversations with students and collaborators, where half of what's said is wrong, and that's fine. And you need some tolerance for looking lost for a while. In our group there is often a period of maybe a few months where, if you asked me what the project was, I couldn't give you a good answer. That phase is uncomfortable but it's where the real work happens.

Then there's a moment of convergence. Suddenly several loose threads connect, and in about a week things that took months become clear. Sometimes the final result looks almost obvious in hindsight, and people will say, "well, anyone could have done this." That's actually the signal of a good result to me. The simplicity at the end is earned by all the nonlinearity before it.

The other thing I'd say is that taste matters more than strategy here. You can't optimize for a paper. If you do, you'll get an incremental result. What you can do is develop a sense for which questions are worth being confused about, and then give yourself permission to stay confused long enough. The best work I've been part of came out of that kind of patience, not from a roadmap.

astra-6.text:
I think the nonlinearity comes from the fact that you don’t really know which observations will become important. You have an idea, you run an experiment, and the result doesn’t quite fit your intuition. At that point, it can look like you’ve made no progress. But sometimes that mismatch is the most valuable thing you’ve found. It gives you a better question.

So there are long periods where you’re accumulating things—failed experiments, intuitions, conversations—and they don’t yet form a coherent picture. Then one result changes how you interpret everything else. The progress looks sudden, but it depends on all that earlier work.

The difficult part is deciding when to persist and when to change direction. I don’t think there’s a formula for that. I try to ask whether an experiment, even if it fails, is teaching me something. If it keeps revealing something I don’t understand, that’s a reason to stay curious. If I’m just repeating the same thing and hoping for a better number, then I probably need to step back.

When you write the paper, you organize it into a clean argument. But that argument is usually something you discovered through the work. It wasn’t necessarily the plan you started with.

r001.rationale: The response describes nonlinear progress and sometimes changing direction, but it does not identify a recurring pattern in Xie’s best research or place a change of direction near the end of a project.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the nonlinear part is that you often don’t know which piece is going to matter when you’re working on it. You might spend a long time trying something that doesn’t work, but that process changes how you understand the problem. Then, much later, a result or a conversation gives you a new perspective, and suddenly those earlier experiences become useful.

So I wouldn’t describe it as having a clear idea and then simply executing it. It’s more like a loop between intuition and evidence. You have an intuition, you run an experiment, and the experiment surprises you. You have to decide: is this just noise, or is it telling me that my original framing was wrong? Sometimes the most productive thing is to change the question.

That’s also why I think you need both persistence and flexibility. You need enough persistence to get past the first disappointing result, but enough flexibility to let go of your favorite explanation. The difficult part is knowing which one the situation calls for. There isn’t a formula for that. You gradually develop judgment by doing the work.

r001.rationale: The candidate says research may involve changing the question, but does not identify a recurring pattern of work coming together after a late-stage change of direction.
